query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A physics‐informed, data‐driven machine learning model that integrates high-throughput ab initio phonon calculations with disorder‐sensitive descriptors (e.g., local bond environments, mass variance, and force constant fluctuations) will more accurately predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) used for thermal insulation than conventional empirical or simplified ab initio methods. This is because the model explicitly accounts for multi-element disorder and its effect on phonon scattering, which traditional approaches tend to average out or neglect.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in an equimolar or near‐equimolar composition state exhibiting extensive chemical disorder.
generation.intervention: Application of a physics-informed machine learning model that incorporates high-throughput ab initio phonon calculations combined with disorder-sensitive descriptors.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under intermediate to high temperature regimes (e.g., 300-600°C) where phonon scattering dominates heat transport, and within composition ranges where the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized compositional fluctuations and bond-strength variations that drive phonon scattering events.
generation.mechanism: By training on a large dataset from ab initio phonon calculations and including descriptors sensitive to configurational disorder, the model captures the diverse scattering mechanisms present in HEAs, thereby reducing the prediction error relative to traditional approaches that assume a uniform lattice.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to predict thermal conductivities that are consistently closer to experimental measurements (e.g., within a 10-15% error margin) and identify HEAs with ultra-low phonon thermal conductivity (below a defined threshold) more reliably than current empirical or standard ab initio methods.
generation.baseline: Existing predictive methods such as empirical correlations or simplified ab initio approaches that typically neglect the full impact of multi-element disorder.
generation.boundary: This predictive improvement is anticipated to apply primarily to single-phase, chemically disordered HEAs within the equimolar or near-equimolar compositional space and may not extend to systems where phase separation or severe short-range order dominates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of prediction improvement over current methods and the precise error margin achievable remain uncertain until further computational validation and comprehensive experimental benchmarking are performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a series of HEA compositions within the equimolar range that are predicted by the model to exhibit phonon thermal conductivities below a specified threshold under controlled temperature conditions. Synthesize these alloys and perform independent thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., using laser flash analysis) in the temperature regime where phonon scattering is prominent.
measurements: High-temperature thermal conductivity measurements of the synthesized HEAs
Characterization of microstructure to confirm single-phase disordered state
Comparison of measured thermal conductivity values against predictions from both the new model and traditional methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured phonon thermal conductivity of the HEAs deviates from the model predictions by more than the acceptable error margin (e.g., >20% difference) or if the model fails to consistently identify compositions with significantly lower thermal conductivity compared to predictions by conventional methods, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. frame.goal: To establish an improved predictive method that accurately identifies high-entropy alloy compositions with low phonon thermal conductivity, thereby enabling better thermal insulation performance.
frame.limitation: Current predictive models (e.g., empirical correlations or simplified ab initio methods) do not fully capture the complex phonon scattering mechanisms in chemically disordered high-entropy alloys, often leading to inaccurate or over-simplified predictions.

decision.trend: Early works tackled HEA properties using simplified first‐principles and empirical models that assumed uniform lattice dynamics, neglecting the full impact of disorder. Later studies introduced more sophisticated treatments – for example, incorporating local spin fluctuations and explicit chemical short-range order via MD/MC and machine‐learning potentials – to capture the nuanced effects of configurational disorder on physical properties. Although these approaches have enabled finer insights into defect dynamics and local ordering, they have not yet fully applied such detailed disorder descriptions to predict phonon-scattering and its impact on thermal conductivity.
decision.unsolved: None of the prior studies directly addresses the challenge of accurately modeling how multi-element disorder influences phonon thermal transport in HEAs. In particular, the limitation remains in quantitatively capturing varied scattering mechanisms that arise from local compositional fluctuations, leading to discrepancies between traditional predictions and experimental observations of thermal conductivity.
decision.lever: Develop a physics-informed machine learning model that integrates high-throughput ab initio phonon calculations with disorder-sensitive descriptors (e.g., local bond environment, mass variance, force constant fluctuations) to predict phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs.
decision.why: This step naturally follows the trend of moving from simplified empirical models to methods that more fully account for configurational complexity. By leveraging abundant computational data and advanced descriptors sensitive to disorder effects, the approach is expected to offer a measurable improvement in prediction accuracy. The model’s performance can then be benchmarked against an experimental threshold in thermal conductivity (e.g., a pre-defined low thermal conductivity value under controlled temperature conditions), providing a decisive test to falsify the hypothesis if the predicted improvement is not realized.
